items.passage: Until 2012, the oldest plant ever regenerated from ancient material had sprouted from a 2,000-year-old date palm seed, so considerably older tissue seemed unlikely to remain ______. Then Svetlana Yashina’s team cultivated flowering Silene stenophylla plants from fruit tissue that Ice Age ground squirrels had stored in Siberian permafrost approximately 32,000 years earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Viable” means able to live and grow. The previous record for growing a plant from ancient material was a 2,000-year-old seed, so tissue many times older seemed unlikely to still be capable of growth. The next sentence shows that this expectation was wrong: Yashina’s team grew flowering plants from tissue about 32,000 years old.

A.why_wrong: “Inert” means lifeless or inactive. Old tissue would be expected to be inert, so saying it seemed “unlikely to remain inert” reverses the logic; the surprise in the text is that ancient tissue could still grow.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns whether the tissue was poisonous; the record and the result it describes are both about growing plants.

D.why_wrong: The squirrels stored the fruit, presumably as food, which makes “palatable,” or pleasant to eat, tempting. But the text sets up a question about whether ancient tissue could still grow, and the answer it gives is that it grew into flowering plants, not that it could be eaten.

sources.what: Yashina et al. 2012 (PNAS): whole fertile Silene stenophylla plants regenerated from about 31,800-year-old fruit tissue from fossil squirrel burrows in Siberian permafrost; previous record 2,000-year-old date palm seeds from Masada

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany). Key B. Negated frame: “seemed unlikely to remain ______,” with the expectation overturned in the next sentence. Distractors: one reversal (inert), one unsupported (toxic), one topic echo (palatable, from the squirrels’ stored food). Rounded: 31,800 years to about 32,000.

items.passage: In the mid-twentieth century, weaving was frequently dismissed as merely decorative craftwork. Anni Albers, however, considered it ______ painting as an art form: she produced what she called “pictorial weavings,” abstract compositions intended to be framed and displayed on a wall rather than used as fabric.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be “on a par with” something is to be equal to it in standing. Albers rejected the idea that weaving was only decorative craftwork and made weavings to be framed and displayed like paintings. This shows she considered weaving equal to painting as an art form.

A.why_wrong: “Subordinate to” means lower in rank than. That describes the dismissive view the text says Albers rejected, not her own view; her pictorial weavings treated weaving as art in its own right.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Albers saw weaving as an introduction or first step toward painting; the text says she made finished weavings to be displayed as art.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Albers thought weaving endangered painting or competed to replace it; the text says she wanted her weavings viewed the way paintings are, as art.

sources.what: Anni Albers made “pictorial weavings,” hand-woven works made as artworks to be hung on the wall, not fabrics for everyday use (Tate exhibition guide)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (textile art). Key D. Clue after the colon restates the key (framed and displayed like paintings, not used as fabric); the contrast with “dismissed as merely decorative craftwork” rules out subordinate to. Distractors: reversal (subordinate to, the dismissive view she rejected), two unsupported (a prelude to, a threat to); a near miss such as indistinguishable from was dropped because, with “as an art form,” it was close to defensible. Mixed frames (on a par with, a prelude to) as in official items with mixed options.

items.passage: Library of Congress librarian Daniel Murray set out to ______ the published work of Black American writers for the 1900 Paris Exposition. Hoping to locate a copy of every book and pamphlet by a Black author, he compiled a bibliography of more than a thousand titles, hundreds of which were subsequently exhibited in Paris.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “inventory” something is to make a complete list of it. The text says Murray tried to find a copy of every book and pamphlet by a Black author and compiled a bibliography, or list, of more than a thousand titles. That effort to record all of these works is an inventory of them.

A.why_wrong: To censor writing is to suppress or remove it. Murray did the opposite: he searched out these works, listed them, and helped put hundreds on public display.

B.why_wrong: Because the works were shown in Paris, “translate” may be tempting, but the text never says Murray put any of them into French; it says he listed and gathered them.

D.why_wrong: To dramatize a work is to adapt it for the stage or to make it seem more exciting. Nothing in the text suggests Murray did either; his task was finding and listing the works.

sources.what: Daniel Murray’s Preliminary List of Books and Pamphlets by Negro Authors (1900): his aim was to secure every book and pamphlet by a Black author for the Exhibit of American Negroes at the Paris Exposition; books from the list were shown there and the list later grew past two thousand titles (sources give 1,100 for the 1900 list)

items.notes: Subject: history. Key C. Restatement in the next sentence (locate a copy of every book, compiled a bibliography). Distractors: reversal (censor), topic echo (translate, from Paris), unsupported (dramatize).

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Because globe skimmer dragonflies (Pantala flavescens) cannot reproduce in the Maldives, islands with almost no freshwater habitat for their larvae, the swarms that appear there each autumn must have ______ open ocean to arrive. Keith Hobson and colleagues supported this conclusion by tracing chemical signatures in the insects’ wings to rainwater in northern India.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “traverse” something is to travel across it. Since the dragonflies cannot have hatched in the Maldives, which lack fresh water for their young, they must have come from somewhere else, and the islands are surrounded by ocean. Hobson’s team traced the insects to northern India, so the swarms must have crossed, or traversed, the open ocean.

B.why_wrong: To skirt something is to go around its edge. The Maldives are islands in the open ocean, so dragonflies coming from India could not reach them by going around the ocean; they had to cross it.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the dragonflies polluted the ocean; the text is about how they reached the islands.

D.why_wrong: To evade something is to avoid it. Dragonflies arriving from India on islands surrounded by ocean could not have avoided the open water; the text’s reasoning requires that they crossed it.

sources.what: Hobson, Anderson, Soto, and Wassenaar 2012 (PLoS ONE): wing hydrogen isotopes of Pantala flavescens migrating through the largely waterless Maldives point to natal origins in northern India

items.notes: Subject: natural science (entomology). Key A. Cause in a Because clause (cannot reproduce in the Maldives), consequence in the main clause (must have crossed the ocean). Near miss: skirted (movement along an edge rather than across).

items.passage: Corals and many other invertebrates house photosynthetic algae inside their own cells, but vertebrate cells were thought to be ______ to such partners, since vertebrate immune systems were assumed to reject them. In 2011, however, Ryan Kerney and colleagues found algae living inside the cells of spotted salamander embryos.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Inhospitable” means unwelcoming, not offering a place to live. The text contrasts invertebrates, whose cells house algae, with vertebrates, whose immune systems were assumed to reject such partners. So vertebrate cells were thought to be inhospitable to algae, until Kerney’s team found algae inside salamander cells.

A.why_wrong: “Receptive” means willing to receive. The text says vertebrate immune systems were assumed to reject algae, so vertebrate cells were thought to be the opposite of receptive; “but” also sets them against the invertebrates that do house algae.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the algae were thought to harm vertebrate cells. The text says the immune system was assumed to keep algae out, which is about the cells rejecting algae, not being endangered by them.

D.why_wrong: “Indispensable” means absolutely necessary. The text never suggests vertebrate cells were thought to be essential to algae; it says such partnerships were thought not to occur in vertebrates at all.

sources.what: Kerney et al. 2011 (PNAS): Oophila algae found inside the cells of spotted salamander embryos; vertebrate immune systems were assumed to bar such intracellular partnerships

items.notes: Subject: natural science (biology). Key C. Contrast (invertebrates house algae, but vertebrates were thought not to) plus received view then finding (however, Kerney found). Distractors: reversal (receptive), two unsupported adjectives that take “to.”

items.passage: Researchers Ovul Sezer, Francesca Gino, and Michael Norton found that humblebragging, or disguising a boast as a complaint (“I’m so tired of being asked to give speeches”), tends to ______. In their studies, people who humblebragged were considered less likable than people who simply bragged.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “backfire” is to have the opposite of the intended effect. People humblebrag to seem modest and likable, but the researchers found that humblebraggers were considered less likable than people who bragged openly. The strategy produces the opposite of what its users want, so it tends to backfire.

A.why_wrong: The text says humblebraggers were considered less likable than people who simply bragged, so the strategy fails at what it is meant to do; it does not succeed.

C.why_wrong: To proliferate is to multiply or spread rapidly. The text says nothing about humblebragging becoming more common; it reports how people react to it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that humblebragging dies out or weakens over time; the finding is about its effect on how much people are liked.

sources.what: Sezer, Gino, and Norton 2018 (JPSP), “Humblebragging: A Distinct, and Ineffective, Self-Presentation Strategy”: humblebraggers are liked less than braggers and the strategy backfires because it seems insincere (HBS Working Knowledge)

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology). Key B. Restatement in the next sentence (judged less likable than plain braggers, the opposite of the aim). The sample complaint is an unattributed illustration, not a quotation from the paper.

items.passage: Filming a runner on a treadmill in slow motion, engineers Christopher Daily-Diamond, Christine Gregg, and Oliver O’Reilly found that the failure of a shoelace knot is remarkably ______. A knot can withstand dozens of strides, but once it begins loosening, it can unravel completely within seconds as the whipping free ends of the laces pull it apart.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Rapid” means happening very quickly. The engineers found that a knot can withstand dozens of strides but, once it begins loosening, can unravel completely within seconds. That quick collapse is what makes the failure rapid.

A.why_wrong: “Gradual” means happening slowly, step by step. The text stresses the opposite: once a knot begins loosening, it unravels completely within seconds.

B.why_wrong: The text does not discuss whether an untied shoelace causes harm; it describes how quickly the knot fails.

C.why_wrong: A knot cannot act on purpose, and nothing in the text suggests anyone unties it intentionally; the failure comes from the runner’s strides.

sources.what: Daily-Diamond, Gregg, and O’Reilly 2017 (Proc. R. Soc. A), “The roles of impact and inertia in the failure of a shoelace knot”: slow-motion video of a runner on a treadmill showed knot failure happens within seconds after gradual loosening (Berkeley News)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (engineering, mechanics). Key D. Restatement in the next sentence (unravel completely within seconds). Distractors: reversal (gradual), two unsupported adjectives.

items.passage: In 1952, Roy DeCarava became the first African American photographer awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship. The fellowship allowed him to ______ an entire year to his own work, and he spent that year photographing everyday life in Harlem, the New York City neighborhood where he was born.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “devote” time to something is to give that time entirely to it. The fellowship let DeCarava spend an entire year on his own photography, and he used the year to photograph daily life in Harlem. So the fellowship allowed him to devote an entire year to his work.

B.why_wrong: The text says DeCarava spent the year photographing Harlem, so he used the year for his own work rather than refusing it.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests DeCarava compared a year with his work; the text says he spent the year doing that work.

D.why_wrong: It makes no sense to say DeCarava borrowed a year to his work, and the text describes the fellowship as an award he won, not something he had to repay.

sources.what: Whitney Museum: in 1952 DeCarava became the first African American photographer to receive a Guggenheim fellowship; he recorded everyday life in his own neighborhood, Harlem

items.notes: Subject: humanities (photography). Key A. Restatement in the clause after the blank (spent that year photographing). Easy key in the official easy range.

fixes: source URL (NGA) returns 403; replaced with the Whitney Museum page, which states the Guggenheim first and the Harlem work

items.passage:
The following text is from Theodore Dreiser’s 1900 novel Sister Carrie. Hurstwood, who has lost his business, is searching the newspaper advertisements for employment.

He scanned the long column, which mostly concerned bakers, bushelmen, cooks, compositors, drivers, and the like, finding two things only which <u>arrested</u> his eye. One was a cashier wanted in a wholesale furniture house, and the other a salesman for a whiskey house. He had never thought of the latter.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “arrested” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “arrested” most nearly means caught. Hurstwood is scanning a long list of job advertisements, and only two of them attract his attention: a cashier’s job and a salesman’s job. To say they “arrested his eye” is to say they caught his eye.

B.why_wrong: “Arrested” can mean detained by the police, but here nothing is held in custody; the text is about two advertisements that drew Hurstwood’s attention.

C.why_wrong: A person who is arrested may be charged with a crime, but advertisements cannot charge someone’s eye. The text describes which job listings Hurstwood noticed.

D.why_wrong: Reading a long column might tire the eyes, but the text says only two listings stood out to Hurstwood, not that they strained his eyesight.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #233, Theodore Dreiser, Sister Carrie (1900), chapter 35; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1900, public domain). Key A. Target arrested in its attention sense, decided by its object (his eye) and by the next sentence naming the two listings. Distractors: two other senses of arrest (detain, charge), one unsupported word from the scene (strained eyes from scanning). Stopped and Halted are not offered.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Max Beerbohm’s 1911 novel Zuleika Dobson. Zuleika, whose beauty has drawn an enormous crowd, has climbed onto the roof of a barge moored on the river.

It looked very cool and gay, this roof, under its awning of red and white stripes. Zuleika moved to the side which <u>commanded</u> a view of the bank. She leaned her arms on the balustrade, and gazed down. The crowd stretched as far as she could see—a vista of faces upturned to her.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “commanded” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “commanded” most nearly means offered. Zuleika goes to the side of the roof from which she can look down at the bank, and from there she sees the crowd stretching as far as she can see. The side of the roof offered, or provided, a view of the bank.

A.why_wrong: “Commanded” often means ordered, but a side of a roof cannot give orders; the text is about what Zuleika could see from that side.

B.why_wrong: A person can command, or earn, respect, but a side of a roof does not earn a view. The text simply says that side looked out over the bank.

D.why_wrong: Something can command, or demand, attention or a high price, but a side of a roof does not demand a view; the sentence describes the view available from that side.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #1845, Max Beerbohm, Zuleika Dobson (1911), chapter on the boat races; excerpt adapted by removing one sentence ("Nests of red and white flowers depended along either side of it.")

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1911, public domain). Key C. Target commanded in its view sense, fixed by its object (a view of the bank) and by the next sentences (she gazed down at the crowd). All three distractors are other senses of command, the most common recipe for meaning items. Original double hyphen rendered as a closed em dash.

fixes: intro said riverboat; in the novel it is a college barge moored by the bank, so now a barge moored on the river

items.passage:
The following text is from G. K. Chesterton’s 1904 novel The Napoleon of Notting Hill. Adam Wayne, the novel’s idealistic protagonist, has been visiting the shops of his London neighborhood.

The man who <u>kept</u> the shop of curiosities had, indeed, enchanted him with a phrase. He was standing drearily at the door of his shop, a wrinkled man with a grey pointed beard, evidently a gentleman who had come down in the world.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “kept” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “kept” most nearly means managed. The man is described as standing at the door of “his shop,” so he is the one who runs the shop of curiosities. To keep a shop, in this sense, is to manage it.

A.why_wrong: To keep something from someone can mean to withhold it, but nothing is being held back from anyone here; the man is standing at the door of the shop he runs.

B.why_wrong: To keep something can mean to save it for later, but the text presents the man as the shopkeeper who runs the shop, not someone storing it away.

C.why_wrong: To keep someone can mean to delay them, as in keeping a person waiting, but here the object is a shop, and the man is the one who runs it.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #20058, G. K. Chesterton, The Napoleon of Notting Hill (1904), Book II, chapter 2; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1904, public domain). Key D. Target kept in its older sense (run a shop), fixed by its object and by “his shop” in the next sentence. All three distractors are other senses of keep. British spelling grey kept as in the source.

items.passage: Cuban filmmaker Sara Gómez’s feature film One Way or Another (1977) is ______ documentary and fiction: its invented love story, acted partly by professional performers, unfolds among real residents of Miraflores, a working-class neighborhood of Havana, who appear on screen as themselves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “A blend of” means a mixture of. The text explains that the film tells an invented love story, partly acted by professional performers, while also showing real residents of a Havana neighborhood as themselves. Combining fiction with documentary material in this way makes the film a blend of the two.

A.why_wrong: The film uses both a fictional story and real people appearing as themselves, so it embraces documentary and fiction rather than rejecting them.

B.why_wrong: A sequel continues an earlier work. The text does not mention any earlier film or story that One Way or Another continues.

D.why_wrong: A review evaluates other works. The text describes how the film combines two kinds of filmmaking, not a discussion of other films.

sources.what: Sara Gómez’s De cierta manera (One Way or Another), completed 1977, mixes documentary and fiction with professional and nonprofessional actors in Miraflores, a Havana housing development

items.notes: Subject: humanities (film). Key C. Restatement after the colon (invented love story among real residents playing themselves). Simplified: Gómez died in 1974 during production and the film was finished by others; not needed for the item.

fixes: Miraflores called a housing project on the edge of Havana; the source says a lower-class neighborhood of Havana, so now a working-class neighborhood of Havana

items.passage: Australian architect Glenn Murcutt designs houses that are highly ______ the local climate. Rather than relying on air-conditioning, his buildings have adjustable louvers, blinds, and wide eaves that residents can open, close, or angle throughout the day to let in cooling breezes and block the hot sun.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Responsive to” means reacting to. Murcutt’s houses have louvers, blinds, and eaves that residents can adjust to let in breezes and keep out the sun. Because the houses can be changed to suit the weather, they are responsive to the local climate.

A.why_wrong: Murcutt’s houses let breezes in and are adjusted to the sun, so they engage with the climate rather than being hidden from it.

C.why_wrong: A house cannot literally be aware of anything, and the text describes buildings designed around the weather, the opposite of ignoring it.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Murcutt’s houses harm the climate; the text says they avoid air-conditioning by using breezes and shade.

sources.what: Lynn Becker on Glenn Murcutt: adjustable louvers inside, slatted blinds outside, natural airflow; of more than 500 houses only two are air-conditioned

items.notes: Subject: humanities (architecture). Key B. Restatement in the next sentence (adjustable louvers and blinds to let in breezes and block sun). Two reversals (hidden from, unaware of), one unsupported (damaging to); easy items often carry two reversals.

fixes: source URL (Britannica) returns 403; replaced with a page that states the louvers, blinds and lack of air-conditioning

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Emily Fairfax and Andrew Whittle found that during wildfires in the western United States, streams dammed by beavers tend to remain green while the surrounding landscape burns, because the water held behind the dams keeps the vegetation moist. These green corridors may therefore help ______ animals from the flames.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “shelter” means to protect or give safe cover. The text explains that beaver-dammed streams stay green and moist during wildfires while the land around them burns. Places that do not burn could give animals somewhere safe to go, so these corridors may help shelter animals from the flames.

A.why_wrong: The text describes green areas that stay unburned, not anything that carries animals away; nothing suggests the corridors remove animals from the fire.

B.why_wrong: It makes no sense to say the corridors distract animals from the flames; the text’s point is that the corridors stay green and do not burn.

C.why_wrong: The researchers measured how green the areas stayed, but the corridors themselves do not measure animals; the sentence is about what the unburned areas can do for wildlife.

sources.what: NASA Landsat: Fairfax and Whittle found beaver-dammed riparian zones keep green, living vegetation during wildfires because pond water keeps plants and soil lush; the patches can act as a refuge for flora and fauna

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Key D. Consequence clue: therefore, after the cause (corridors stay green and moist while the land burns). Three unsupported distractors, the easy-tier pattern; measure is a mild topic echo of the satellite study. The animal-refuge idea is stated as a possibility (may), as in the source.

fixes: source (UMN record) did not state the animal-refuge premise the key hinges on; replaced with the NASA Landsat article, which does
passage said the dams spread water across the valley floor; both sources say the dams store water, so now the water held behind the dams

items.passage: French designer Charlotte Perriand’s two years in Japan, beginning in 1940, ______ the furniture she created there. For example, after noticing a pair of sugar tongs fashioned from bamboo, she reinterpreted her celebrated steel chaise longue, a reclining chair, in bamboo.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “shape” something is to influence its form. The example shows Perriand noticing bamboo sugar tongs in Japan and then reinterpreting her steel chaise longue in bamboo. Her time in Japan therefore shaped the furniture she created there.

B.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that Perriand’s time in Japan held up her work; the example shows her making new furniture there.

C.why_wrong: The text does not say her stay replaced the furniture she made; it shows how what she saw in Japan influenced that furniture.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Perriand’s stay hid her furniture from view; the text describes how a bamboo object she noticed led her to remake a chair.

sources.what: Charlotte Perriand arrived in Japan in 1940 and left in 1942; bamboo sugar tongs she saw in Tokyo led her to remake her steel chaise longue in bamboo (Pen magazine)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (design). Key A. Example-pinned: For example introduces the instance that shows influence. Three unsupported distractors (easy pattern).

items.passage: Indian filmmaker Ritwik Ghatak repeatedly ______ the 1947 partition of Bengal in his work. His films Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960), Komal Gandhar (1961), and Subarnarekha, for example, all portray the lasting upheaval caused when the region was divided between India and what became East Pakistan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “revisit” a subject is to return to it again. The text lists three of Ghatak’s films, all made years after 1947, that each portray the upheaval the partition caused. Since he came back to the partition in film after film, he repeatedly revisited it.

A.why_wrong: The films listed came out in 1960 and 1961 and later, long after the 1947 partition, so they could not have predicted it.

B.why_wrong: The films portray the “lasting upheaval” the partition caused, which suggests it is treated as a painful event; nothing in the text suggests Ghatak praised it.

D.why_wrong: The text gives several films that all deal with the partition, so Ghatak did not avoid the subject; he returned to it again and again.

sources.what: Ritwik Ghatak’s Partition trilogy, Meghe Dhaka Tara (1960), Komal Gandhar (1961), and Subarnarekha, about the aftermath of the 1947 partition of Bengal and the people it displaced (Scroll.in)

items.notes: Subject: humanities (film). Key C. Example-pinned: three films instantiate repeated treatment. Subarnarekha left undated (sources give 1962 and 1965).

fixes: B celebrated replaced with praised: celebrated can also mean commemorated in art, a second sense close to the key, and the swap brings the batch key-longest rate to the official range

items.passage: Tallying the 1880 US census by hand took years, and officials feared that the 1890 count might not be completed before the next census began. Herman Hollerith’s tabulating machine, which detected holes punched in cards, made tallying far less ______: an operator could process approximately 7,000 cards daily, at least ten times faster than by hand.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Laborious” means requiring a great deal of time and effort. Counting by hand took years, while Hollerith’s machine let an operator process approximately 7,000 cards a day, at least ten times faster. The machine therefore made tallying far less laborious.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about mistakes in the count; its point is how much faster the machine was, so there is no reason to think it made tallying less accurate.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the machine made tallying more chaotic; an operator feeding cards through a machine thousands of times a day describes a quicker, not a less orderly, process.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests the machine made the results of tallying harder to foresee; the text compares how long the work took by hand and by machine.

sources.what: Computer History Museum: estimates warned the 1890 census would not be finished before the 1900 census began; an average operator processed about 7,000 cards a day, at least ten times faster than manual methods

items.notes: Subject: history (technology). Key B. Negated frame (far less ______) with the clue after the colon (ten times faster). Kept to the source: the 1880 count took years (sources say seven to eight); no six-week figure.

items.passage:
The following text is from Lafcadio Hearn’s 1904 short story “Yuki-Onna.” Minokichi, a young woodcutter, and Mosaku, an old woodcutter, have taken shelter from a snowstorm in a ferryman’s hut, where a mysterious woman dressed in white has just appeared and vanished.

He called to Mosaku, and was frightened because the old man did not answer. He <u>put out</u> his hand in the dark, and touched Mosaku’s face, and found that it was ice!
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “put out” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “put out” most nearly means extended. In the dark, Minokichi cannot see Mosaku, so he reaches toward him and touches his face. To put out a hand in this sense is to extend it, or stretch it out.

A.why_wrong: “Put out” can mean to douse, or extinguish, a fire or a lamp, and the mention of the dark makes this tempting. But Minokichi puts out his hand and then touches Mosaku’s face, so he is reaching, not putting out a light.

C.why_wrong: To put someone out can mean to inconvenience them, but here the object is Minokichi’s own hand, which he uses to touch Mosaku’s face.

D.why_wrong: To put out a book is to publish it, a sense that has nothing to do with a man reaching for his companion in a dark hut.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #1210, Lafcadio Hearn, Kwaidan: Stories and Studies of Strange Things (1904), “Yuki-Onna”; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story, 1904, public domain). Key B. Phrasal target put out in its physical sense, fixed by the object (his hand) and the next action (touched Mosaku’s face). All three distractors are other senses of put out; Doused is the most tempting because of “in the dark.” Single-word options, as the phrase target allows (M2 covers an underlined phrase or phrase options).

items.passage: Older adults typically retrieve words and names more slowly than younger adults do, a lag usually taken as evidence of cognitive decline. Linguist Michael Ramscar and colleagues contend that the lag is instead largely ______ accumulated knowledge: decades of reading and conversation expand the vocabulary stored in memory, and searching a larger store of words simply takes more time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: An artifact of something is a result or by-product of it. Ramscar and colleagues explain the slower retrieval by the size of what older adults know: a bigger store of words and names takes longer to search. So the lag, usually read as decline, is largely a by-product of how much they have learned.

A.why_wrong: A bulwark is a defense. The text does not present slower retrieval as protecting against learning; it presents learning as the cause of the slowness.

B.why_wrong: An antidote counteracts something harmful. Nothing suggests that the lag counteracts what older adults have learned; the lag results from it.

D.why_wrong: A precondition must be in place before something else can happen. The text runs the relation the other way: the learning comes first and produces the lag, not the lag making the learning possible.

band7_moves: familiar key in a transferred sense (artifact as a misleading by-product)
clue is a mechanism the student must turn into dependence
near miss on direction (a precondition for)
all four options past rank 10,000

In a 2012 study, Andres Arce and colleagues determined that larvae reared with lysozyme, a bacteria-killing enzyme in these secretions, were nearly twice as likely to survive, demonstrating that the secretions ______ the developing young.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To benefit someone is to help them. Larvae raised with a substance from the secretions were nearly twice as likely to survive, so the secretions help the young beetles.

A.why_wrong: The secretions nearly doubled the larvae’s chances of survival, so they help the young rather than harm them.

C.why_wrong: The secretions coat the carcass and kill bacteria; nothing suggests that they hide the larvae from anything.

D.why_wrong: To adorn is to decorate. The secretions kill bacteria and help larvae survive; nothing suggests they decorate anything.

sources.what: Arce, Johnston, Smiseth and Rozen, “Mechanisms and fitness effects of antibacterial defences in a carrion beetle” (Journal of Evolutionary Biology, 2012): parental anal secretions are bactericidal; secreted lysozyme increases larval survival nearly two-fold

items.notes: Subject: natural science (insect behavior). Key letter B. Cause clue: the survival result (“showing that”).

items.passage: Hale Woodruff’s Amistad murals, painted in 1939 for the library of Talladega College in Alabama, ______ the principal events of the 1839 rebellion aboard the slave ship Amistad: one panel shows the captive Africans seizing control of the vessel, a second presents their trial in a US courtroom, and a third illustrates their eventual return to Africa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To depict something is to show it in a picture. Each panel shows one part of the Amistad story, from the revolt to the trial to the return to Africa, so the murals depict its major events.

B.why_wrong: The panels show the events, so the murals reveal them rather than conceal them.

C.why_wrong: The murals were painted a century after the 1839 revolt, so they could not predict its events.

D.why_wrong: Paintings cannot delay events that had already happened; the murals show them.

sources.what: Talladega College archives, The Amistad Murals: Hale Woodruff’s panels for Savery Library (1939) showing the revolt, the trial, and the return to Africa

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting, history). Key letter A. Example-pinned: three panels after the colon.

items.passage: Researchers A. Peter McGraw and Caleb Warren propose that people find a situation humorous when it seems wrong in some way yet simultaneously harmless. Such “benign violations,” they suggest, can take ______ forms: slapstick threatens a person’s dignity, malapropisms break linguistic conventions, and peculiar behavior defies social norms.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Varied means of different kinds. The examples come from different areas of life, a person’s dignity, language, and social behavior, so benign violations take varied forms.

A.why_wrong: The three examples differ from one another, so the forms are not identical.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests these violations are hidden; slapstick and strange behavior are out in the open.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when these kinds of humor arose.

sources.what: McGraw and Warren, “Benign Violations: Making Immoral Behavior Funny” (Psychological Science, 2010): humor requires a situation appraised as a violation and as benign at once; violations of personal dignity (slapstick), linguistic norms (malapropisms), social norms (strange behaviors) and moral norms

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology of humor). Key letter C. Example-pinned: three different kinds of violation after the colon.

items.passage: In 1958 Yanktonai Dakota artist Oscar Howe submitted a painting to an annual exhibition of Native American art at the Philbrook Art Center in Oklahoma. The judges rejected it, deeming it “not Indian,” but Howe did not ______ their judgment: in a letter to the museum, he argued that Native artists deserved the freedom to develop individual styles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To accept a judgment is to go along with it. Howe wrote to the museum arguing against the narrow standard the judges applied, so he did not accept their judgment.

A.why_wrong: Howe wrote a letter arguing against the judges’ standard, so he did question their judgment.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Howe forgot the decision; his letter responds to it directly.

D.why_wrong: The text does not concern who announced the decision; it describes how Howe responded to it.

sources.what: American Indian magazine (Smithsonian NMAI), “An American Modernist: Oscar Howe Fractured Stereotypes of Native Art”: his 1958 painting Umine Wacipi was rejected from the Philbrook Indian Annual as “not Indian”; his letter argued for Native artists’ freedom to develop individual styles

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting, history). Key letter B. Negated frame “did not ______”; clue after the colon.

items.passage: Economists Michela Giorcelli and Petra Moser found that after Lombardy and Venetia adopted copyright law in 1801 under French rule, the two states’ output of new operas rose far faster than that of other Italian states. Since later extensions of copyright terms brought no comparable gains, basic protection, not its prolongation, appears to have been ______ creativity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A spur to something is an incentive that drives it on. Copyright arrived in Lombardy and Venetia under French rule, and afterward the two states’ production of new operas rose far faster than elsewhere in Italy, so the protection encouraged composers’ work. Because later extensions brought no further gains, the text credits basic protection, not longer terms, with that effect.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that copyright took the place of creative work; the law and a rise in new operas went together.

B.why_wrong: A constraint on creativity would hold it back, but opera output rose faster after the law was adopted, not more slowly.

D.why_wrong: A symptom of creativity would be a result of it. The law came with French rule, and the rise in new operas followed it, so the protection preceded the creativity rather than reflecting it.

sources.what: NBER Digest (May 2020) on Giorcelli and Moser: Lombardy and Venetia adopted copyright in 1801 after coming under French rule; new operas rose sharply there relative to other Italian states; more durable and popular operas; no comparable benefit from longer copyright terms

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the rise follows the law, and the law came from conquest, so protection drove output; then reject the reverse direction). Corrected ranks: substitute 9,221; constraint 9,447; spur 6,779; symptom 16,017. Band 6 (plain phrase keys, reasoning carries the item). Detail simplified: output figures (threefold against about 50 percent) given as 'far faster'.

band7.why: Raw ranks a spur to 6,779; a substitute for 9,221; a constraint on 9,447; a symptom of 16,017: 1 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 3.99 (the band-6 mean). Plain phrase key with the reasoning carrying it, as the band-6 B6 items do: the student maps basic protection to the 1801 law and rejects the reversed direction (a symptom of). Constraint falls to one stated fact. A band 6 as targeted, on the weaker side.

items.passage: Studying professional basketball and soccer teams, organizational behavior researcher Roderick Swaab and colleagues found the link between a team’s share of top players and its success to be ______: adding stars helped only up to a point, after which coordination suffered and results declined. In baseball, where players depend less on one another, additional talent never hurt.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A nonlinear relationship is one that does not change at a steady rate in one direction. The text says that more top players improved results only up to a point and then made them worse, so success first rose and then fell as talent increased.

B.why_wrong: An inverse link would mean more talent always brought less success. In basketball and soccer, success rose with talent at first and fell only past a certain point.

C.why_wrong: A spurious link is one that only appears to exist. The text reports a real pattern in which talent first helped and then hurt; nothing suggests the connection was illusory.

D.why_wrong: A proportional link, in which success rises steadily with talent, is closer to the baseball pattern, where extra talent never hurt. In basketball and soccer, results declined once teams had too many stars.

sources.what: APS press release on Swaab, Schaerer, Anicich, Ronay and Galinsky (2014), Psychological Science: top talent helps team performance only up to a point in basketball and soccer, then hurts as coordination suffers; not in baseball

items.notes: Subject: social science (organizational psychology). Key letter A. Restatement after the colon, read as a shape (rise then fall). Two distractors each fit half the pattern (inverse, the decline; proportional, the rise and baseball). Raw ranks: nonlinear 72,820; inverse 49,909; spurious 20,718; proportional 68,085 (corrected about 15,600; 20,900; 20,700; 17,800). Band 6.

band7.why: Raw ranks nonlinear 72,820; inverse 49,909; spurious 20,718; proportional 68,085 (corrected about 15,600 to 20,900): check 1 passes, but three of the four are school mathematics words a 1400 scorer knows, so the rarity is a corpus artifact (check 6 finds at most one unknown word). One-step colon restatement read as a shape, two half-right distractors. Band 6 as targeted.

items.passage: Asgard archaea, identified in 2015 from DNA dredged up near an Arctic Ocean hydrothermal vent, carry many genes otherwise associated with complex cells, and some biologists consider them the closest living relatives of those cells’ ancestors. Until Hiroyuki Imachi and colleagues grew one in the laboratory after twelve years of effort, however, any picture of the organisms themselves was ______.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Conjectural means based on inference rather than direct evidence. Before Imachi’s team grew one of these microbes, Asgard archaea were known only from DNA, so any idea of what the organisms themselves were like had to be inferred from their genes rather than observed.

A.recipe: near miss: false rather than unproven (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: Fallacious means mistaken. The text says the organisms had not been grown and observed, not that earlier ideas about them turned out to be wrong.

B.why_wrong: Incontrovertible means beyond dispute. Knowledge drawn only from DNA, before anyone had grown the organism, is the opposite of settled.

C.why_wrong: Perfunctory means done with little care or interest. Nothing suggests that biologists were careless; the limit was that the organisms had never been grown.

band7_moves: option set all past rank 14,000 (rare words throughout)
blank on the earlier, superseded state, with the finding given only as the turning point (until ... however)
implicit clue: knowledge from DNA alone implies an inferred picture, never stated
near-synonym distractor failing on one feature (fallacious: false, not unproven)

sources.what: Science News on Imachi et al. (2020, Nature): Asgard archaea found in 2015 from genetic material from an Arctic Ocean hydrothermal vent; many eukaryotic genes; argued to be closest living relatives of the archaea that gave rise to complex life; about 12 years of lab work to grow one

items.notes: Subject: natural science (microbiology). Key letter D. Contrast frame (however) with the blank on the earlier state of knowledge; the clue is implicit: DNA alone means any picture of the cell was inferred. Corrected ranks: fallacious 42,005; incontrovertible 36,669; perfunctory 14,278; conjectural 41,050: all four past 10,000, mean log about 4.5. Band-5 guard: clear (key not the lone rare option). Near miss: fallacious (false rather than unverified).

band7.why: Raw ranks fallacious 42,005; incontrovertible 36,669; perfunctory 14,278; conjectural 41,050: 4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000, mean log 4.49; band-5 guard clear. B3 shape of 6c9f1727 (Until ... the thing was notional): blank on the earlier state of knowledge, the clue implicit (known only from DNA, the organisms themselves not yet grown). Fallacious is the near miss that fails on one feature (false, not unproven), incontrovertible the reversal, perfunctory a rare unsupported word.

items.passage: Kernza, a perennial grain that The Land Institute developed from intermediate wheatgrass, need not be replanted each year, and its deep, dense roots help build healthy soil, but it is unlikely to ______ annual wheat anytime soon: even under ideal conditions, it yields only about 30 percent as much grain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To supplant something is to take its place. Kernza has real advantages, but it produces only about 30 percent as much grain as wheat even under ideal conditions, so it is unlikely to replace annual wheat as a crop in the near future.

A.why_wrong: To complement wheat is to add to it alongside it. A lower yield is a reason Kernza cannot replace wheat, not a reason it could not be grown in addition to wheat.

C.why_wrong: Whether Kernza looks like or resembles wheat is not discussed, and its lower grain yield has nothing to do with resemblance.

D.why_wrong: Kernza is perennial and does not need replanting each year, so it already outlasts annual wheat; saying it is unlikely to outlast wheat contradicts the text.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Kernza: intermediate wheatgrass grain developed by The Land Institute; perennial; deeper and more abundant roots support healthy soil; as much as 30 percent of the yield of traditional wheat under ideal conditions

items.notes: Subject: natural science (agriculture). Key letter B. Negated frame stated plainly (unlikely to), as in 3.21; the colon gives the reason, which the student must connect to replacement rather than to coexistence. Raw ranks: complement 19,388; supplant 28,305; resemble 11,654; outlast 39,183 (corrected complement about 9,400, resemble about 10,100). Band 6.

band7.why: Raw ranks complement 19,388; supplant 28,305; resemble 11,654; outlast 39,183 (corrected complement about 9,400, resemble about 10,100): 3 of 4 past 10,000, but resemble, outlast and complement are familiar words. Plain negated frame (unlikely to) with the reason after the colon, the band-6 B5 pattern of bbb77c84 (superseded). Band 6 as targeted.

fixes: notes: the ranks labelled corrected were raw; relabelled and added corrected values for complement and resemble

items.passage:
The following text is from Ford Madox Ford’s 1915 novel The Good Soldier. The narrator, an American, recalls the years that he and his wife spent in the company of an English couple, the Ashburnhams.

So began those nine years of uninterrupted tranquillity. They were characterized by an extraordinary <u>want</u> of any communicativeness on the part of the Ashburnhams to which we, on our part, replied by leaving out quite as extraordinarily, and nearly as completely, the personal note. Indeed, you may take it that what characterized our relationship was an atmosphere of taking everything for granted.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “want” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “want” means lack. The narrator says that he and his wife answered the Ashburnhams by “leaving out quite as extraordinarily” the personal note, so the Ashburnhams too must have held back from sharing anything personal. The friendship was marked by a deficiency of communicativeness, not by any desire for it.

B.why_wrong: “Want” can mean a strong desire, but the narrator describes the Ashburnhams as uncommunicative, a quality he and his wife matched by leaving out the personal note; nothing suggests the Ashburnhams longed to communicate.

C.why_wrong: “Want” can mean poverty, but the sentence concerns how little the Ashburnhams shared about themselves, not a lack of money.

D.why_wrong: “Want” can mean a pressing need, but the text does not say communication was urgently required; it says it was almost entirely missing.

band7_moves: familiar word in an older secondary sense (want as lack), everyday sense offered as a distractor
clue a clause away, in the narrator’s ironic matching of the couple’s reserve
every distractor a real sense of the target (desire, poverty, need)
option set all past rank 20,000; key a mid-frequency word, not a plain synonym

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #2775, Ford Madox Ford, The Good Soldier (1915), part I, chapter IV; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter A. Older secondary sense of a common word (want as lack) against its everyday sense (desire); the clue is the narrator’s parallel clause (replied by leaving out ... the personal note). All three distractors are real senses of “want” (desire, poverty, need). Corrected ranks: deficiency 23,080; hankering 21,045; indigence 63,234; exigency 32,335: all four past 20,000. Literary work not used in any official item (no Ford in material/rw).

band7.why: Raw ranks Deficiency 23,080; Hankering 21,045; Indigence 63,234; Exigency 32,335: 4 of 4 past 20,000, mean log 4.50, rarer than both CB band-7 M1 models (6557f7fc, 7f935017). Common target in its older sense (want as lack) against the everyday sense (Hankering), and two need senses (Indigence: poverty; Exigency: pressing need) that fail on one feature each. The clue is the parallel clause (we replied by leaving out the personal note). The "want of any" frame helps a reader who knows "for want of", the one thing keeping it from the top of band 7.

items.passage: Colombian artist Oscar Muñoz’s installation Aliento (1995–2002) consists of small oval mirrors that appear entirely conventional until viewers lean in and exhale onto them. At that moment the mirrors no longer ______ the individuals peering into them: as condensation clouds each surface, the viewer’s own image disappears, replaced by a photographic portrait of someone who has died.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To reflect a person is to show that person’s image, as a mirror normally does. Once a viewer exhales onto one of Muñoz’s mirrors, the viewer’s own image disappears and a portrait of someone else appears, so the mirror stops showing the person looking into it.

A.why_wrong: Breathing on the mirror makes the viewer’s image disappear, so the mirrors do obscure the viewers at that moment; saying they no longer obscure them contradicts the text.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the mirrors ever made viewers look better than they are; the change described is that the viewer’s image disappears entirely.

C.why_wrong: The text says viewers lean in and exhale onto the mirrors; it says nothing about the mirrors ceasing to fascinate the people who look into them.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Oscar Muñoz (artist): Aliento (Breath), 1995–2002, small oval mirrors screen printed with grease; when a viewer breathes on one, the viewer’s reflection is erased and a portrait of a dead person, taken from newspaper obituaries, appears

items.notes: Subject: humanities (visual art). Key letter D. Negated frame (no longer), with the clue after the colon; the key is the everyday function of a mirror, which the student must see the work suspend. Corrected ranks: obscure 5,213; flatter 8,339; captivate 31,527; reflect 5,527. Detail simplified: the portraits are of people who died in Colombia’s political violence (not stated).

items.passage: Shilai Zhang and colleagues determined that from a single planting, the perennial rice variety PR23 produced grain for eight consecutive harvests over four years, averaging 6.8 metric tons per hectare per harvest. These results made its productivity ______ that of conventional annual rice, which averaged 6.7 metric tons but required replanting for every crop.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be on a par with something is to be about equal to it. PR23 averaged 6.8 metric tons per hectare per harvest and conventional annual rice averaged 6.7, so the perennial rice was about as productive as the annual rice it was compared with.

A.why_wrong: PR23 was bred from other rice, but the sentence compares the size of two yields; one variety’s productivity is not produced from another’s.

C.why_wrong: A fraction of annual rice’s productivity would be much smaller, but 6.8 metric tons is about the same as 6.7.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that PR23’s productivity depended on how much annual rice produced; the two were simply measured and compared.

sources.what: Zhang et al., Sustained productivity and agronomic potential of perennial rice, Nature Sustainability (published online November 2022): from a single planting, perennial rice produced grain for eight consecutive harvests over four years, averaging 6.8 Mg per hectare per harvest versus 6.7 Mg for replanted annual rice

items.notes: Subject: natural science (agriculture). Key letter B. Restatement by numbers: the student compares 6.8 with 6.7. Corrected ranks: derived 2,000 or so (derive); par 12,383; fraction 12,184; contingent 17,762. Mixed phrase frames, as in 2.20.

items.passage: Canadian artist Brian Jungen’s Prototypes for New Understanding (1998–2005) are masks hand-stitched from disassembled Nike Air Jordan sneakers and shaped to recall the mask designs of coastal nations of British Columbia. Jungen exhibited them on metal armatures inside transparent display cases, much as anthropology museums have traditionally displayed Indigenous artifacts, making their presentation ______ that museum convention.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: An allusion to something is an indirect reference to it. The text says Jungen showed his sneaker masks on metal armatures (supporting frames) inside transparent display cases, “much as” anthropology museums have traditionally displayed Indigenous artifacts, so his presentation deliberately called that museum convention to mind.

A.why_wrong: A departure would be a break from museum practice, but Jungen used the same method museums use: objects on metal supports inside clear display cases.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Jungen’s presentation got in the way of the museum convention; it borrows that convention.

D.why_wrong: A precursor comes before what it leads to, but the museum convention is described as traditional; Jungen’s works came later, from 1998 to 2005.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Brian Jungen: Prototypes for New Understanding (1998–2005), masks made from Nike Air Jordan sneakers, evocative of mask designs of coastal nations of British Columbia; early works shown as if anthropological artifacts, on metal armatures inside Plexiglas vitrines

items.notes: Subject: humanities (visual art). Key letter C. The similarity is stated (much as); the student must choose the word for a deliberate reference to that convention. Revised after a blind solve: the earlier version left the museum display practice to outside knowledge. Corrected ranks: departure 1,837; obstacle 8,054; allusion 6,623; precursor 38,574.

items.passage: In 1964 landscape architect Cornelia Hahn Oberlander persuaded Vancouver’s municipal government to ______ the driftwood logs that had washed up on its beaches. Rather than burning the logs, the city kept them at her insistence and put them to use as seating and shelter for visitors to its shoreline.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To repurpose something is to give it a new use. Instead of being burned, the driftwood logs were kept and put to use as seating and shelter for visitors, a use quite different from their former place as debris.

B.why_wrong: To incinerate is to burn, which is exactly what the city did not do; the logs were kept rather than burned.

C.why_wrong: To restore something is to return it to an earlier condition. The logs were not repaired or returned to any former state; they were put to a new use.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the logs were sold; the city kept them on its beaches for public use.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Cornelia Oberlander: in 1964 she persuaded Vancouver to keep driftwood logs for seating and shelter instead of burning them

items.notes: Subject: humanities (landscape architecture). Key letter A. Restatement in the next sentence (kept rather than burned, used as seats and shelter). Corrected ranks: repurpose unseen (modern); incinerate unseen; restore about 5,000; auction 11,781.

fixes: precision: the clue now says the city put the logs to use as seating and shelter (source: kept them and reused them as benches and shelters); before, the logs only "over time came to serve", which made repurpose the best word by elimination rather than a precise fit

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sarah Grand’s 1897 novel The Beth Book. Beth, who is twelve, has gone to stay with her great-aunt Victoria.

Aunt Victoria was surprised herself to find how kindly Beth <u>took to</u> a regular life, how exact she was in the performance of her little housekeeping duties, and how punctual in everything; she had never suspected that Beth’s whole leaning was towards law and order.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “took to” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Aunt Victoria is surprised by “how kindly” Beth took to a regular life: Beth turns out to be exact in her housekeeping duties and punctual in everything, because her “whole leaning” is toward law and order. So Beth readily adapted to an orderly routine.

A.why_wrong: “Took to” can mean fled into, as in taking to the woods, but Beth is not escaping anything; she is settling comfortably into an orderly routine.

B.why_wrong: “Took to” can mean carried someone to a place, but nothing is being carried here; the phrase describes Beth’s response to a way of living.

C.why_wrong: “Took to” can mean turned to out of need, but Beth is not driven to a regular life by desperation; she takes to it “kindly,” because it suits her leaning toward order.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook #28088, Sarah Grand, The Beth Book (1897), chapter XXII; excerpt copied exactly except that the sentence is ended after “law and order”; Beth is twelve and travels with Great-Aunt Victoria Bench in chapter XXI

items.passage: In the summer of 2011, a Sargassum seaweed bloom large enough to be detected in satellite imagery appeared in the tropical Atlantic Ocean for the first time. Since then, the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt has become ______: composed of numerous floating patches, some covering an acre, it was estimated to weigh 24.2 million tons in June 2022.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Enormous means extremely large. After the colon, the text says the belt is composed of numerous patches, some covering an acre, and that it was estimated to weigh 24.2 million tons, which shows how huge it has become.

A.why_wrong: Scarce means hard to find. A belt of seaweed weighing 24.2 million tons is the opposite of scarce.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the seaweed being easily damaged; it describes the belt’s size.

D.why_wrong: The text does not discuss whether the belt’s appearance or size can be predicted; the information after the colon is about how large it is.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt: in summer 2011 a bloom large enough to be noticeable in satellite imagery appeared for the first time; many patches, some up to an acre; in June 2022 the belt was estimated to weigh 24.2 million tons

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oceanography). Key letter B. Restatement after the colon (patches up to an acre, 24.2 million tons). Corrected ranks: scarce about 5,000; enormous about 2,500; fragile 9,404; predictable unseen (modern, easy).

items.passage: Physician Rebecca Lee Crumpler wrote A Book of Medical Discourses (1883) for mothers and nurses rather than for fellow physicians, and the book places particular emphasis on ______. Crumpler encouraged readers to understand the structure of the human body, arguing that many ailments have identifiable causes that can be eliminated before the ailments ever develop.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Prevention means stopping something before it happens. Crumpler wanted readers to understand the body so that the causes of many ailments could be eliminated before the ailments developed, so her book emphasizes preventing illness.

A.why_wrong: Surgery belongs to medicine, but the book was written for mothers and nurses, and the text describes keeping illness from starting, not operating on patients.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text describes the book as focused on scientific research; it gives readers practical knowledge of the body.

D.why_wrong: The text does not say Crumpler stressed following orders; she urged readers to understand the body for themselves.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Rebecca Lee Crumpler: A Book of Medical Discourses (1883) written for nurses and mothers; emphasized the possibilities of prevention; urged women to understand the structure of the body; every ailment has a cause that can often be removed

items.notes: Subject: history (medicine). Key letter C. Restatement in the next sentence (causes removed before ailments develop). The item hangs on the book, not on Crumpler’s firsts. Corrected ranks: surgery 19,358; research 2,475; prevention 32,906; obedience 4,121.

items.passage: Toshio Mori’s short story collection Yokohama, California, which portrays the everyday experiences of Japanese Americans, was scheduled for publication before World War II, but the war ______ its release: the collection did not appear until 1949, accompanied by an introduction from the celebrated writer William Saroyan.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Delayed means made later than planned. The collection was supposed to come out before World War II but did not appear until 1949, so the war pushed its release back.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the war paid for the book; the text says only that the book came out years later than planned.

B.why_wrong: The text does not say the war gave Mori the idea for the stories, and the blank concerns the book’s release, which came years late.

C.why_wrong: Accelerated means sped up, but the release was scheduled before the war and did not happen until 1949.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Toshio Mori: Yokohama, California had a tentative publication date, but World War II halted publication; published in 1949 by Caxton Printers with an introduction by William Saroyan; his stories portray everyday lives of Japanese Americans

items.notes: Subject: humanities (literature, publishing history). Key letter D. Restatement in the next sentence (did not appear until 1949). Corrected ranks: funded 7,219; inspired 3,563; accelerated 30,748; delayed 2,128.

items.passage: In a 2005 experiment, cognitive scientists Petter Johansson and Lars Hall asked participants to identify the more attractive of two faces, then secretly handed them the photograph they had rejected. Most participants failed to notice the substitution. Instead, they readily ______ the choice they had never made, explaining, for instance, that they preferred blondes when they had actually selected a dark-haired woman.

items.passage: Victorian commentators warned that penny dreadfuls—sensational serialized stories sold in weekly one-penny installments to young working-class readers—bred crime; one 1893 editorial declared that such fiction “makes thieves of the coming generation.” Many historians, however, consider the stories largely ______, and some suggest that they may even have helped improve literacy among the very readers critics feared they would corrupt.

items.passage: In rope-pulling experiments published in 1913, French agricultural engineer Max Ringelmann found that individual efforts are not ______ in a group. items.passage: Because a dollar of tax saved is equally valuable whether it reduces a payment or increases a refund, standard economic models predict that taxpayers minimizing their liability should be ______ which outcome they anticipate. D.why_wrong: Being wary of something means being cautious or suspicious about it. The models’ prediction rests on the equal value of a saved dollar in either case and says nothing about taxpayers’ caution; it implies the outcome should not matter to their decisions at all.
